title: The Slate
passages:
The Marrow lay bow-to a sea that kept arriving, and everything on her deck that wasn't lashed was trying to leave. Wren knelt in the lee of the wheelhouse with her back to the wind, the reader in her lap — a scuffed orange box the size of a bread loaf, a full-face mask coiled off one side of it. Her forearm had stopped bleeding into her sleeve and started bleeding onto the case. She wiped it on her trousers without looking.

"Sit down, Captain."

Sol sat, on the winch drum, hands in her lap like a woman at a bus stop. "You going to tell me what the box does, or do I guess?"

"It reads slates." Wren turned her collar down. Set in the skin at the collarbone, in a bed of yellow resin the size of a playing card, was the slate: the glass that takes down everything a diver sees and hears for as long as she stays under. "Yours is furred over. Hold still, this is the part you complain about."

She got a thumbnail under the resin and peeled it back in one curl, clipped the lead, and felt the reader wake up against her knees.

"It builds what's on there into something your head will take. You watch it through the mask, you get your hours back. The ones it caught. Not the ones it didn't — the slate's the only witness aboard and it's a bad one, it only writes down what was in front of your face."

"And if it wasn't in front of my face?"

"Then far as the boat's concerned it didn't happen."

Teo was rasping behind her. Not crying. Just the long wet haul of a boy whose scrubber — the cartridge that eats the carbon out of a breath — had an hour left in it, generous. Nia had him inside her coat and her chin came up like a dog's when Wren glanced back.

Wren checked the glass in its brass case on the bulkhead. The needle had walked off the bottom of the weather she'd read at dawn. "Factor's barge left the mole forty minutes back," she said. "Heard him tell somebody he was coming to collect."

"Collect what," Sol said. "Hold's empty."

"No," Wren agreed. "It is."

Dey was coiling drum line, slow and cheerful, stacking loops on his forearm like a man with all night and nothing planned. Twelve thousand gone out of the year he had left to buy, and he looked rested about it.

While the build spun up, Wren pulled Dey's log. She kept her voice flat, the way she did for the crew, and said the true thing out loud for once. "Your splice held. Cut went in at 06:12, verified, checksum clean. I took the name out of your build and it stayed out."

"Good," Dey said, agreeable.

"So you didn't keep it because I missed it. You kept it because you kept it."

"I don't know what I kept," Dey said. "It's nice not knowing."

Sol watched Wren's hands on the box. "So you're the one who tells people who they are."

"I hand people their own hours. What they do with them is their business."

"That isn't what I asked."

"No," Wren said. "It isn't."

The box chirped and text started crawling up its little screen, the transcript it wrote as it worked, naming every voice it knew. In the wheelhouse the radio muttered on the backup channel, open, unanswered, the way it had been open since noon.

"Salas," Dey said, easy, to nobody, the way a man reads a label off a tin.

Wren looked at the screen.

SALAS. 00:00:04.

Four seconds into her captain's day. Timestamped before Sol went over the side, before the drone, before the choice, before anyone aboard the Marrow had said that name out loud.
